title: Chapter 6 — The Street
paragraphs: If I'd been astonished at first seeing someone as outlandish as Queequeg strolling through the polite society of a civilized town, my surprise quickly vanished during my first daylight walk through New Bedford's streets.

Near any major port's docks, you'll regularly encounter the strangest-looking characters from foreign lands. Even on Broadway and Chestnut Street, Mediterranean sailors sometimes startle the ladies. London's Regent Street isn't unfamiliar with Lascars and Malays; and in Bombay, live Yankees have often frightened the locals. But New Bedford outdoes them all. In those other haunts you see only sailors; in New Bedford, actual cannibals stand chatting on street corners — genuine savages, many still carrying unholy flesh on their bones. It makes a stranger stare.

But besides the Fijians, Tongans, Erromangans, and other South Sea islanders, and besides the wild specimens of the whaling trade who stagger unnoticed through the streets, you'll see even more curious sights. Every week, scores of fresh young Vermonters and New Hampshire boys arrive, all hungry for fortune and glory in the whale fishery. They're mostly young and powerfully built — men who've felled forests and now want to trade the axe for the whale-lance. Many are as green as the Green Mountains they came from. In some ways, they seem only hours old. Look at that fellow strutting around the corner: he wears a beaver hat and a tailcoat, cinched with a sailor's belt and sheath-knife. Here comes another in a sou'wester and a shabby cloak.

No city-bred dandy compares to a country-bred one — a real backwoods dandy, the kind who mows his field in buckskin gloves to avoid tanning his hands. When a country dandy like this decides to make his name and joins the great whale fishery, you should see what he does when he reaches the seaport. Ordering his sea outfit, he requests bell-buttons on his waistcoat and straps on his canvas trousers. Ah, poor Hay-Seed! How bitterly those straps will burst in the first howling gale, when you're driven, straps, buttons, and all, down the throat of the storm.

But don't think this famous town has only harpooneers, cannibals, and country boys to show its visitors. Not at all. Still, New Bedford is an unusual place. If it weren't for us whalemen, this stretch of land might still be as desolate as the coast of Labrador. As it is, parts of the surrounding countryside look almost skeletal. The town itself is perhaps the most expensive place to live in all of New England. It's a land of oil, certainly — though not like Canaan, a land of milk and honey. The streets don't flow with milk; in spring they aren't paved with fresh eggs. Yet despite this, nowhere in all America will you find more aristocratic houses, more magnificent parks and gardens. Where did they come from? How were they planted on this once barren ground?

Go and look at the iron decorative harpoons around that grand mansion, and your question will be answered. Yes, all these beautiful houses and flowery gardens came from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans. They were harpooned and dragged up here from the bottom of the sea.

In New Bedford, fathers give whales as dowries for their daughters and set aside a few porpoises for each niece. You have to visit New Bedford to see a brilliant wedding; they say every house has reservoirs of oil, and every night they recklessly burn the finest spermaceti candles.

In summer, the town is beautiful — full of fine maple trees, long avenues of green and gold. In August, the magnificent horse-chestnuts hold up their tapering, upright cones of blossoms like candelabras to every passerby. So powerful is human art; in many parts of New Bedford, it has planted bright terraces of flowers on the barren refuse rocks cast aside on creation's final day.

And the women of New Bedford bloom like their own red roses. But roses bloom only in summer; the fine color of their cheeks is perennial as sunlight in the seventh heaven. Nowhere else can you match that bloom — except in Salem, where they say the young women breathe such perfume that their sailor sweethearts can smell them miles offshore, as if they were approaching the fragrant Moluccas instead of the Puritan sands.
